chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
title: Schools in Homestead and the Ward
summary: She attended the Fourth Ward School and others, lived on a street near the mill; the Hill versus the Ward.

blocks.x: Well, I went to school in Homestead, but I also went to school in some of these other little towns, too. So my education was sort of split between Homestead -- my early education -- and among some of these little towns around the valley around Homestead.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Which was the main school you attended, can you give us the name of it?

Well, I started out at a school called the Fourth Ward School and we moved and I went to another school, Second Ward School in Homestead. And of course when I graduated from elementary school I went to Homestead High which was up on 12th Avenue -- we lived for the most part below 8th Avenue and Homestead was the main street. We lived below 8th Avenue in a lot of different places.

I was born in a little alley-like between two streets called Goldway, 538 Goldway. And I spent a lot of my early youth in what they called The Ward, this would be below 8th Avenue -- 4th Avenue, 2nd Avenue.

My grandmother, my father's mother, her barber shop was on a street called Dixon Street which was between 4th and 5th Avenues in Homestead.

So I spent most of my time -- in the War I guess you would say --
What was the significance of it having that name -- The Ward?

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

I don't know, unless it meant closer to the mill because the mill was -- the Monongahela River came through Homestead. The mill was right on the River and the first street would be Second Avenue, and Third Avenue, Fourth Avenue and right up. The distinction was between the Ward and the Hill. If you lived above Eighth Avenue you lived on the Hill. If you lived below Eighth Avenue you lived in the Ward. I have no idea what the significance was. It might have been a political division for some reason that I wouldn't know about.
Would there be a corresponding division of wealth -- with the better off people living on the Hill?

Yeah, because I suppose when the mill was established most of the houses in the Ward would have been considered company property, you know, the houses that they set up for the workers. There were a few of what I might say private dwellings of individual families that lived in the Ward, especially -- let's see, Homestead is about eight streets wide and City Farm Lane was the first street, you know,

where the mill -- the mill was sort of like L-shaped so City Farm Lane, so the farther you got away from City Farm Lane the more residential it would appear to be, but the other properties were set up for the workers in the mill and what you might say multiple dwellings, but I don't suppose there was any building there that had any more than four or five families in it.
Is that what your step-father did, work in the mill?
So he would have been a newcomer to Homestead?
